title: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom
summary: Anansi is given a pot holding all the wisdom in the world, and discovers that the pot is much easier to fill than it is to carry.
moral: Wisdom carried alone is a pot too heavy for one back.
attribution: A traditional Ashanti tale, retold for Ubuntu Tales.

cover.alt: A spider with a clay pot climbing a tall tree, web lines radiating across the forest

sentences.text: Nyame, the sky god, kept all the wisdom in the world in a clay pot.
Anansi the spider came to the sky and talked so long and so well that Nyame agreed to lend him the pot.
“Only mind you do not spill it,” said Nyame, “for there is no second pot.”
Anansi carried the pot home and put it on the ground very carefully.
He sat down beside it and thought about how he was now the wisest creature in the world.
Then he thought that he should hide the pot where no one else could find it, and he decided that a very tall tree was the best hiding place in the forest.
He tied the pot to his stomach and began to climb.
But a spider climbing a tree with a pot on his stomach can only see his own feet, and his feet were behind the pot.
He slipped.
The pot swung.
He gripped with three legs and could not move.
He tried to climb with the pot on his back, and could not do that either, because his back was a spider’s back.
His small son, Ntikuma, came along the path and watched him for a while.
“Father,” he said at last, “why do you not tie the pot behind you, and climb face-up, so that you can see where you are going?”
Anansi stopped.
He was furious, because the advice was good and it had come from a child who still had his first teeth.
He was so angry that he dropped the pot.
It broke on the roots of the tree, and every scrap of wisdom in the world scattered into the forest.
Now wisdom is not lost.
It lies where it fell: in the roots, in the riverbank, in the market, in the mouths of children.
That is why no one person has all of it, and why we must keep telling stories to one another, if only to collect what the pot spilled.
